title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text: This was a group project. The goal was to predict whether a collegiate athlete is at risk of injury, using 800 athletes and 18 physiological and performance measurements. Each teammate built and tuned a different set of models, and we compared the results.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text: This was a group project. The goal was to predict whether a collegiate athlete is at risk of injury, using 800 athletes and 18 physiological and performance measurements. Each teammate built and tuned a different set of models, and we compared the results.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
The question
Can physiological and performance data predict which athletes are at higher risk of injury, and which type of model does it best?

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
My role
I built and evaluated five supervised classification models in R: k-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA), Naive Bayes, and logistic regression. My teammates built support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, and neural network models, and I benchmarked my results against theirs.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
Data and method

Exploration and preparation. I explored the data and standardized the features so that measurements on different scales could be compared fairly.
Tuning. I tuned each model’s hyperparameters using 10-fold cross-validation and grid search.
Interpretation. I looked at the coefficients to see which features were linked to higher injury risk.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
Results
QDA performed best on validation data, with 97.5% accuracy, so I selected it as my final model. On a held-out test set, it reached 96.25% accuracy. The test set is data the model never saw during training or tuning, so that second number is the more honest estimate of how it would perform on new athletes.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
Tools
R, supervised classification, cross-validation, grid search, feature standardization.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text: This project had two parts. In the first, I queried a multi-table relational database of Olympic results to compare medal totals across 162 countries. In the second, I scraped IMDb’s Top-250 movie list and compared how ratings changed between 2004 and 2025.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text: This project had two parts. In the first, I queried a multi-table relational database of Olympic results to compare medal totals across 162 countries. In the second, I scraped IMDb’s Top-250 movie list and compared how ratings changed between 2004 and 2025.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
The questions

How do Olympic medal totals compare across countries?
Have the ratings of IMDb’s top-rated movies gone up or down over time?

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
Data and method
Olympic data (SQL). The data was spread across several related tables, so I wrote SQL queries with joins and subqueries to bring the medal results together by country.
IMDb ratings (web scraping). I built an automated scraping pipeline to collect the Top-250 list for 2004 and for 2025, then compared the ratings between the two years. The raw titles came from unstructured HTML, so I used regular expressions to clean and standardize more than 250 movie titles so the lists could be compared.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
Results
Between 2004 and 2025, 61% of the movies showed an improved rating.
I put the findings into publication-ready visualizations and a written statistical report.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
Tools
SQL, web scraping, regular expressions, data visualization.

title: World Population Growth Estimation
text: I wanted to estimate how fast the world population is growing using data pulled directly from the web, rather than a file I downloaded once. The project covers collecting the data, cleaning it, estimating annual growth rates, and measuring how uncertain those estimates are.

title: World Population Growth Estimation
text: I wanted to estimate how fast the world population is growing using data pulled directly from the web, rather than a file I downloaded once. The project covers collecting the data, cleaning it, estimating annual growth rates, and measuring how uncertain those estimates are.

title: World Population Growth Estimation
text:
The question
What is the annual growth rate of the world population, and how confident can I be in my estimate?

title: World Population Growth Estimation
text:
Data and method
Collecting the data. I wrote R functions that scrape real-time population data from web APIs. The functions include error handling, so one failed request does not break the whole run.
Working with XML. I automated data extraction from 64 XML files, parsed the ISO 8601 timestamps, and used the dates to run a time series analysis.
Measuring uncertainty. A single growth-rate estimate says nothing about how reliable it is. So I ran Monte Carlo simulations with more than 10,000 iterations. A simulation repeats the estimate many times with random variation, and the spread of the results gives a confidence interval.

title: World Population Growth Estimation
text:
Results
My estimates came within 5% of official population projections.

title: World Population Growth Estimation
text:
Tools
R, web APIs, XML parsing, Monte Carlo simulation, time series analysis.

title: Brady Shaw
text:

I work with R, Python and SQL, and my projects cover relational database analysis, web scraping and data cleaning, Monte Carlo simulation, machine learning, and regression modeling. I like turning messy data into clear answers that someone can act on.
